    NVIDIA reportedly halts AI chip shipments to Southeast Asia

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (396 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Companies like Dell have stopped shipping server hardware to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia.
    • Sources indicate that NVIDIA has reportedly put a stop to shipments of AI server hardware to four Southeast Asian countries.
    • In recent years, Chinese AI labs have turned to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia to gain access to NVIDIA's most powerful chips.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Companies like Dell have stopped shipping server hardware to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia.

    Sources indicate that NVIDIA has reportedly put a stop to shipments of AI server hardware to four Southeast Asian countries. According to The Financial Times, a handful of the company's manufacturing partners, including Dell and Supermicro, told clients in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia that the chipmaker is not allowing their server orders to be sent to them. The Financial Times reports it's unclear if the halt is temporary. The news comes just days after NVIDIA reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive.

    In recent years, Chinese AI labs have turned to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia to gain access to NVIDIA's most powerful chips. They used a gap in US export controls by renting access through cloud compute providers that bought servers with NVIDIA GPUs inside. In recent weeks, the US Commerce Department moved to close that loophole. First by introducing new rules aimed at stopping that exact practice, and second by targeting Megaspeed, the company at the center of the NVIDIA scandal.

    On Wednesday, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its "Entity List." Companies, including NVIDIA, now need a US license to ship goods covered by US export rules to Megaspeed. Huang had resigned from his position on November 12 after reports surfaced that he had engaged in multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive that some US officials suspect was a Chinese intelligence asset. Megaspeed had leased access to NVIDIA chips to Chinese companies. The Justice Department is also investigating whether Megaspeed broke US export rules.

    It has been revealed that under the newly introduced US rule, data centers that were already providing large amounts of computing power to companies based in China or other location covered by the rule have 90 days from November 19 to get a license if they want to keep doing so. "There's this new rule but no guidance on execution," one cloud executive told the outlet. "No one knows how to apply for this license while the 90-day clock is ticking. It's causing sheer chaos in the region." Demand from Chinese tech companies led to a data center construction boom in Southeast Asia. NVIDIA booked $104 billion in revenue through its Singapore subsidiary in 2025, representing a 72 percent increase from the year before.

    #150440. From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3632 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3632 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ars Technica is a place that has always leaned into remote working.
    • As Ars staffers step away from their desks for a few days to spend some time with family and friends, we wanted to give you a look inside our home offices.
    • Recent findings suggest that as an apartment dweller in New York City, I’ve usually set up my home work station in a small corner of my residence along with sometimes decamping for local cafes or coworking spaces.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ars Technica is a place that has always leaned into remote working. Since its beginnings in 1998, Ars has never had a single, central office—a setup that makes for a great commute to work, with little risk of getting stuck in traffic.

    As Ars staffers step away from their desks for a few days to spend some time with family and friends, we wanted to give you a look inside our home offices. We’ve got all sorts of setups, tucked into basements, dens, spare bedrooms, apartment corners, and lofts. They run the gamut from minimalist “here’s my laptop and monitor” setups to “I really like collecting things.” Without any further ado, let’s dig in:.

    Recent findings suggest that as an apartment dweller in New York City, I’ve usually set up my home work station in a small corner of my residence along with sometimes decamping for local cafes or coworking spaces. My current hodgepodge of equipment is probably on the minimal side compared to many members of the Ars team.

    I’m usually multitasking on my basic monitor display and work laptop configuration, with the monitor sitting on a stack of several books (apologies in particular to Mary Beard’s excellent history of the Roman Republic, titled SPQR).

    In a recent development, accessories plugged into the work laptop include a simple Lekvey Ergonomic Mouse and a Logitech K380 keyboard that I’ve often brought along with me to public workspaces. Sometimes I’ll use the built-in Macbook Air keyboard, but I like having the laptop display elevated, whether I’m working at home or elsewhere.

    My personal Apple M4 Macbook Air usually sits on the side, where I primarily use my old, battered pair of Sennheiser HD 518 headphones to listen to music during the work day.

    In a recent development, I have a simple standing desk, but it’s not the easiest to change positions, so I wouldn’t recommend it for anyone who wants to adjust frequently. Whenever I’m sitting, I sometimes switch between a simple wooden chair from Ikea and a more ergonomic chair.

    Aside from an assortment of coasters and a tea container turned pen holder, my desk also holds a painted dinosaur sculpture (courtesy of my young son) and two versions of the Spot It! Matching game (also for my son’s entertainment).

    In a recent development, last but not least, I have a pair of Powerblock dumbbells tucked under my work desk. I wouldn’t say they feature heavily in my work day, but they’re easily accessible if I have 15-20 minutes to spare.

    Greetings from my basement hobbit hole! My desk sits across from a workbench area that was already here when we got the house. I have labeled drawers full of PC parts, tools, and cables accumulated over decades. The drawer organization was quite the upgrade over my previous solution of “chuck everything in unlabeled storage tubs.”.

    According to recent reports, my current PC setup is an AceMagic W1 mini PC running Fedora, and a Blackview Intel N150 I keep on Windows for audio recording (PipeWire is fussy). The two are connected to my inputs and monitors via a KVM so I can switch back and forth at the press of a button.

    Industry observers note that the monitors are mismatched thrift finds. One is an HP, the other Sansui. The TV is a similar story—an old Samsung LCD that set me back $10 at the thrift store. I use it as a third monitor for watching PC streams. An Onn Android box is also connected, though it rarely earns its keep.

    Below the TV sits a Lenovo ThinkSmart View, a repurposed B2B video-conference gadget modded to run LineageOS. It handles smart-home controls and tracks my solar production during the day. There’s also a Flashforge 5M printer in the corner, and the pegboard wall holds tools, Mega Man figures, and about 10 years’ worth of convention badges.

    The back closet is the scary part: old consoles, spare drives, boards, and parts for every project I’ll get to “eventually.” The chair is a Dowinx gaming chair I grabbed on a Slickdeals whim—it’s fine, but I wouldn’t recommend it to anyone.

    The rug-patterned Dude mousepad really ties the desk together, man.

    According to recent reports, I’m something of an outlier at Ars, in that I use Windows most days. I’m no great lover of Windows 11, but I still use it thanks to years of computing inertia. My machine is custom, built in early 2024 with a Raptor Lake Core i7 (that thankfully did not fall victim to the overvolting bug) and an RTX 4070 Ti. It has long been my preference to build my own PC for gaming and work to ensure easier repairs and upgrades. Although with the prices of components being what they are, I hope all these parts last a very long time.

    According to recent reports, the primary monitor on the bottom is an Alienware ultrawide OLED. I got it for gaming, but it’s also a nice productivity display that gives me lots of room to keep windows visible. Above that, I have an Asus ProArt LCD calibrated in sRGB for photography work. I’ll get to the keyboard, but I do want to point out my preferred mouse, a Logitech MX Vertical. I have carpal tunnel issues, and this thing has been a lifesaver.

    In a recent development, I believe organizing my desk before taking the photo would be a form of lying, so rest assured this is what it looks like on an average day. I have a few organizers to keep phones and various accessories from getting scattered around my Uplift sit-stand desk (seen here in sitting mode), which I quite like. The chair is a Herman Miller Aeron, which I don’t like as much. It’s fine and has plenty of adjustments, but the mesh is very hard. You should only buy one on sale, and if you do, get a cushion.

    Above the desk are some Star Trek cross-stitches, courtesy of my talented wife. The dangling ’90s-era computer components are a mobile I put together many years ago, featuring a neat Intel i486 DEC socket board and some SDRAM.

    I’m not a particularly neat person. My natural state is to have two or three projects half-exploded all over every surface: piles of 3D-printed prototypes, spools of wire, a soldering iron, laser-cut acrylic for a pinball project, the packaging from something I recently opened and need to sort through. Those aren’t random examples; that’s the contents of my workbench behind me on the opposite wall of my office as I type this. It’s a bit of a mess.

    To combat that tendency, I make a concerted effort to keep the desk where I spend so many hours of the day calm and a place where I can focus. It doesn’t always last! But I’m always at least striving for it, and what I find helps is having a very intentional design where everything has a place.

    My desk surface is made from rubberwood butcher block, on Flexispot motorized legs. I recently picked up another rubberwood slab to build the cantilevered shelf. The supports neatly tuck away my M1 Max Mac Studio, which is still a great little workhorse with 64 gigs of RAM, and my Arturia audio interface, which I use to record line-in sources like synthesizers.

    According to recent reports, on the left is a task lamp and a pen holder with six discrete holes. This fits in with the intentional design part: I have to pick the six things I want handy, and I can’t just pack it with more and more stuff. Presently that’s my Apple Pencil, a Pentel mechanical pencil, an Olfa mini snap-off blade knife, and a selection of three Pigma Micron pens in different line widths.

    The right side holds an Aiyima 10th anniversary hi-fi stack: A20 amp, D20 DAC, and T20 pre-amplifier. The speakers are SVS Ultra Evolution Nanos. They’re sitting on the latest version of some 3D-printed stands I’ve been designing. I print them with hollow legs and then fill them with concrete for mass and stability.

    Since I know Ryan is going to flex on everyone with his keyboard collection, I have to try my best to keep up with my daily driver. It’s a Percent Canoe v2 case, running Holy Panda switches modified with 63 gram SPRiT springs for a slightly lighter touch, and GMK Bento keycaps. This was a pandemic build project, and it has served me well since.

    According to recent reports, I used to run multiple monitors, but I’ve found that I don’t focus as well with them and prefer a singular spot to pay attention to. I’m using an Apple Studio Display because I’m very picky about pixel density. I opted to order it without the stand so I can run it on an ergo arm.

    When I built the shelf for my desk, I fabricated a mounting bracket for the arm out of schedule 40 steel pipe and a 3D-printed sleeve that sits in a pocket CNC’d out. Since it sits flush on the underside, I don’t have to use a clamp that would extend down into the space where I keep my Mac and audio interface.

    Recent findings suggest that when I need a secondary display, or I want to use my Apple Pencil in Photoshop or Illustrator, I use an iPad Pro. I used to have a dedicated Wacom monitor, but I find this much more convenient both in terms of space efficiency and ergonomics. If I’m not really leaning into hand drawing or lettering, I do most of my graphic work with a mouse, which is presently a Logitech MX Master 3S.

    To wrap up the final items, the chair is an Aeron I bought new in 2003. I’ve had to repair it a few times over the years, but it’s either been things I consider wear items (wheels, armrests, gas cylinder) or Herman Miller has replaced under warranty. It was a significant purchase for me at the time, but it’s ended up being a great investment. That’s Sophie draped over it, one of our four cats.

    Tucked next to my desk, behind the subwoofer under the little side table, is my home server and networking gear. The server runs Unraid and is primarily used for my Jellyfin media collection and Home Assistant. Networking is a combination of Unifi and Eero, but at some point I’d like to ditch the Amazon gear and go fully native Unifi.

    I spend a lot of time in my office. It’s not just a place to edit, write, and do other Ars-y things. It’s also my rehearsal space and a place to relax and unwind when I need some me-time. Long-time readers won’t be surprised to see Apple hardware front and center. I’ve been using Macs since college, and they’ve done alright by me ever since. My daily driver is a first-gen Mac Studio (M1 Max) with 64GB of RAM, which drives two Apple Studio Displays. As a long-time mouse hater, I use a Magic Trackpad along with my extended Apple keyboard. Underneath the desk is a UPS and a Thunderbolt disk enclosure that is one of my two backups.

    The bookshelves are where my home networking gear lives. That includes a Synology DS920+ that backs up all of the computers in the house, serves up media, and runs my instance of Mealie. The Eero 6+ handles home networking, with everything in my office except my MacBook Pro connected via Ethernet. As much as I’d like to live a paperless existence, the HP printer-scanner-copier combo still gets some use. They’re difficult to see, but to the right of the G4 Cube (sadly inoperable) on top of the bookshelf sit an Apple TV and M2 Mac mini, which hook up to the 43-inch TV. My graphite iBook and eMate are now resigned to propping up bibs from races and other cycling events.

    This is my office, which is the place where I am much of the time. The chair is a Herman Miller Embody and is one of the best things I’ve ever spent money on. The desk is a standy desk that I don’t stand at nearly often enough; the work PC is a Mac Studio; and the gaming PC is a frankenbox with a cockpit running Windows 10 LTSC (from my cold dead hands, etc., etc.). The Linux boxen are headless and are mostly banished to the closet.

    The paintings (including the awesome Apollo 12 SCE-to-aux one) are all originals by the inimitable Stephen Quick, who does a hell of a job with commissions. What started as a funny idea about a Warhol-esque take on the many faces of Kurt Russel kinda turned over a couple of years into somewhat of a “these are some actors whose work I like” series. My buddies and I went to a lot of movies when we were teenagers, so the imagery sparks good memories for me.

    Industry observers note that the rest of the office has space stuff in it, especially the part behind where I was standing to do the pano sot. I’ve heard it said that when a man hits his 40s, he must choose between becoming obsessed with World War 2 history or smoking meats; I did kind of a variation on “World War 2” and fell deeply into historic human spaceflight. Apollo is kind of my jam, and some weekends you can even catch me docenting at Space Center Houston’s Saturn V exhibit! (Yeah, it’s maybe not as pretty as the exhibits at Marshall or KSC, but the JSC Saturn V is the only one made of flight stages end to end!).

    Sources indicate that welcome to the mess of wires, monitors, and handheld fidgets that is my loft desk. Let’s take a quick tour along with the rest of my gaming cave/mid-life crisis Mario collection that lives right by it.

    In a recent development, my office setup is probably a lot simpler—basic?—than most of my Ars colleagues. I use an adjustable wood-top desk that allows me to stand or sit while I work. I do almost all of my writing and editing on a MacBook Air, and I have a spare available in case I need it. Sometimes I travel with both MacBooks so I can use one for writing and the other for monitoring a rocket launch, press conference, or other event. I also work a lot from my porch, where I can enjoy the fresh air and quiet mornings on our ranch in rural Texas.

    Recent findings suggest that an iMac and a second monitor stand behind the laptops. I generally use them to watch conferences, rocket launch livestreams, weather radar, or live news. It just depends on what’s happening any given day. One of the things I love about the space beat is there’s something happening nearly every day, and it’s possible to cover much of it from home. There are often multiple things happening the same day, so the dual-screen setup becomes especially handy then. For example, I can use one monitor to watch what SpaceX is doing at Starbase, Texas, and another to watch a rocket launch in Florida. I use a ring light behind my desk for TV interviews or podcast appearances.

    It has been revealed that absent from my desk is my large collection of space swag stowed away in storage boxes. Perhaps I will bring it out to add to my workspace for a future Ars Staff Source. For now, I use a mouse pad from the European Space Agency that I’ve had for at least 15 years. The mouse pad features ESA’s astronomy missions that were in development or operations at the time. All of the missions have now launched, and some have long been decommissioned. It’s a good reminder of how long it takes to design, develop, build, and launch science missions. Anyone who claims this stuff is easy is being dishonest.

    This image is a bit misleading, in that it implies I work on the pictured PC (RTX 4070, Ryzen 5 3600X, 32GB RAM) and sit at my desk while doing so. That’s occasionally true, but more often, I can be found wandering around my apartment with my M4 MacBook Air during work hours. I don’t even sit at my desk to game much anymore—on the off chance that I’m playing a game the Steam Deck can’t handle natively, I’ll stream it from my PC to my Steam Deck using Moonlight and Apollo (previously Moonlight and Sunshine).

    Recent findings suggest that you may also notice that my desk, from a tech giant called Uplift, is adjustable. As it turns out, I don’t enjoy standing while working, so the ability to loft my tabletop skyward has been chiefly deployed in the service of making it easier to retrieve something I’ve dropped down there.

    Industry observers note that at night, my desk often moonlights as a craft area; I swap out my keyboard (a Wobkey Rainy75) for a cutting mat, and I’m ready to build some Gundam, assemble a book nook, or tackle a crochet pattern (a few amigurumi are scattered around my desk to keep me company). You can see some of my supplies on the left, but I have other stuff stashed in drawers and various containers that I can bring to my desk as needed.

    So sure, I do work here sometimes.

    Industry observers note that my wife Anna and I rent an apartment in Chicago, and we’ve chosen the city life over, well, space. As such, my 10-by-10-foot office space serves multiple functions. I use it primarily for work, but since Anna and I are both major gamers and she is often camped out with the PlayStation 5 in the living room, I have my own gaming setup in the office. It’s cramped, but it works!

    I do editing, news hits, and most other work during the day, but I’m a night owl at heart and find that I can only do heavy writing—like on longer feature articles—at night, so I’m picturing both the daytime and nighttime view here. I have a collection of Govee lights (Govee Hexa panels, several RGB Edison bulbs, and a Star Light Aurora galaxy projector) to max out the vibes for those nighttime focus (and gaming) sessions.

    We moved into this place in the dead of the pandemic, and I bought most of the stuff in this office during that year or shortly afterward, so it’s a very 2020–2021-coded array of hardware.

    The desk is a Secretlab Magnus Pro, and the chair is a Steelcase Gesture. I love the desk, but I have mixed feelings about the chair. I don’t like the material of the Herman Miller Aeron, but people kept telling me to buy an ergonomic chair for long-term back health, so I bought the other one everyone recommends. To be frank, I’m never fully comfortable in it, though, and wish I had just said “life is short” and bought something comfy and bad for me!

    It has been revealed that the main machine is a 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M1 Max, 64GB of RAM, and a 2TB hard drive—still holding strong after five years. I also have an Alienware Aurora R10—hear me out—prebuilt gaming desktop with a Ryzen 9 5900X and an RTX 3080. When I bought it, it was during the COVID-times GPU shortage, and there was absolutely no other way to get the GPU I wanted. The system is loud, hot, and hard to work with; I want very much to replace it with something custom, but the need has not yet arisen. I tend to hold on to stuff until it literally stops working.

    As for monitors, the center monitor is a 27-inch, 1440p, 240 Hz OLED Asus XG27AQDMGZ. The left and right monitors are both 27-inch 4K, 60 Hz IPS Dell U2720Qs. I’ve got a pair of Audioengine A2+ speakers, plus a Blue Yeti X, a Logitech Lighta Glow, and the good ol’ Logitech C920 for video and voice calls.

    Sources indicate that then there’s input: a Keychron K1 Pro keyboard, a Razer Orochi V2 mouse, and a Sony DualSense controller. I’ve got a Belkin charging station for my iPhone 17 Pro, AirPods Pro, and Apple Watch Series 7, plus AirPods Max on a headphone hanger on the front of the desk. The CalDigit E5 Thunderbolt hub is doing a lot of work here!

    I feel fortunate to have a job that allows me to occasionally apply my lifelong love affair with video games. My favorite game of all time is The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim (Morrowind is a close second), and I like Bethesda games in general. I’ve got a working (but mostly useless) Fallout Pip-Boy, which ought to count for something! I also have a few other Skyrim knickknacks hanging about. And if you’re a Star Trek: The Next Generation viewer, you might have already noticed the desk mat.

    Recent findings suggest that I do enjoy playing games at my desk sometimes, but after I sit at the computer all day, I often want to be somewhere else when winding down. So pictured here is the other half of the room. The leather armchair I use for console gaming is paired with a leather ottoman (the colors don’t match because, again, COVID-era supply limitations).

    I have an LG C1 OLED TV with a PlayStation 5 Pro, a PlayStation 3 that is backward-compatible with PlayStation 1 and 2 games, a Nintendo Switch I barely touch, and three Analogue FPGA retro consoles: the Super Nt, Mega Sg, and 3D.

    It’s a tiny room to spend so much time in, but after almost seven years in this apartment, it certainly feels like home!

    💡 Key Takeaways

    Tech Report: Ex-Kenyan governor jailed for 25 years over pregnant girlfriend's murder

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It is rare for such a high-ranking official to face public criminal trials in Kenya.
    • A former Kenyan governor has been jailed for 25 years for the murder of a university student who was seven months pregnant with his child.
    • The High Court on Friday sentenced Zacharia Okoth Obado, the former governor of Migori County, along with two former aides, over the 2018 killing of Sharon Belyne Otieno.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It is rare for such a high-ranking official to face public criminal trials in Kenya.

    A former Kenyan governor has been jailed for 25 years for the murder of a university student who was seven months pregnant with his child.

    The High Court on Friday sentenced Zacharia Okoth Obado, the former governor of Migori County, along with two former aides, over the 2018 killing of Sharon Belyne Otieno.

    The investigation established that an "intimate relationship" had existed between Obado and Otieno, which "subsequently led to a pregnancy with the deceased that the governor was unhappy about".

    Both Obado and Otieno's legal teams remarked they would appeal against the sentence.

    His former personal assistant, Michael Oyamo, was also sentenced to 25 years in prison, while former county clerk Caspal Ojwang' Obiero received an 18-year sentence.

    The court found that Obado had provided the motive and financial resources for the murder, while Oyamo coordinated its execution and Obiero provided logistical support and helped conceal the crime.

    Judge Cecilia Githua said Obado's absence from Migori at the time of the killing did not absolve him of responsibility.

    She rejected the prosecution's request for the death penalty, as well as Obado's plea for a non-custodial sentence.

    Otieno, 26, was killed between 3 and 4 September 2018 after leaving a hotel in Rongo, south-western Kenya, with journalist Barrack Oduor.

    She had contacted Oduor to discuss her relationship with the then-governor. The two were abducted shortly afterwards.

    Oduor managed to escape by jumping out of a moving vehicle. His account of the abduction became a crucial lead in the investigation.

    Otieno's body was later found near Kodera Forest.

    A post-mortem examination found that she had died from strangulation and excessive bleeding caused by multiple stab wounds.

    The court also established that Obado was the biological father of her unborn child.

    Obado and his co-accused were convicted of murder on 23 July 2026, following a lengthy trial in which prosecutors called 42 witnesses and presented 81 exhibits.

    On Friday, the court declined to award compensation to Otieno's family, saying there was insufficient evidence to establish the financial losses they had claimed.

    Before sentencing, Otieno's mother had appealed to the judge not to send Obado to prison, saying his imprisonment would amount to "another death in the family".

    She urged the court to consider a non-custodial sentence, arguing that Otieno's three children, from different relationships, needed his support.

    But the judge said the family's circumstances could not override the court's responsibility to impose an appropriate punishment.

    Otieno's family, through their lawyer Antony Opondo, told Kenya's Daily Nation that they would file an appeal seeking Obado's acquittal.

    Otieno's murder sparked protests and renewed public debate about violence against women in Kenya.

    A national survey found that at least 34% of women had experienced physical violence in 2022.

    The case has also drawn attention because it is rare for such senior political figures to face public criminal trials in Kenya.

    Obado served two terms as governor of Migori County in western Kenya, switching allegiance between a smaller political party and the region's dominant opposition movement.

    He later backed President William Ruto and formally joined his ruling party in 2023, becoming a regional organiser.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that what happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt?
    • Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of consumers.
    • Recent findings suggest that the attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases, claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that what happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the initiative is to auction them off to the highest bidder.

    Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of consumers.

    Recent findings suggest that the attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases, claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements mentioned.

    Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted. It is unclear what the buyer’s aims are for the chats.

    In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, Latest York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through.

    Industry observers note that “Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta remarked in a statement.

    Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model.

    In a recent development, “Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said. “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their company into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.”.

    Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.”.

    Sources indicate that the opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs. They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to people’ chats. The deal has not yet received final court approval. (Disney also agreed to hire most of Character.ai’s remaining staff.).

    Character.ai suffered after its co-founders, Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, returned to Google, when the tech giant signed a non-exclusive license to use the AI startup’s tech. The company also faced lawsuits related to child safety — one involved the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother claimed he had become obsessed with a chatbot on the platform.

    California AG Bonta is joined in the effort to oppose the sale of Character.ai user data by attorneys general from Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and West Virginia.

    • Protests are planned in Los Angeles and Chicago, while a union called for strikes at 11 Amazon sites in Germany.
    • Amazon workers and their supporters are once again set to go on strike and hold protests in more than 20 countries across the Black Friday and Cyber Monday period.
    • Teamsters are planning protests on Cyber Monday (November 30) in Los Angeles and Chicago.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Protests are planned in Los Angeles and Chicago, while a union called for strikes at 11 Amazon sites in Germany.

    Amazon workers and their supporters are once again set to go on strike and hold protests in more than 20 countries across the Black Friday and Cyber Monday period. Trade union federation UNI Global remarked the workers are pushing Amazon to negotiate with unions and respect employees' right to organize.

    Teamsters are planning protests on Cyber Monday (November 30) in Los Angeles and Chicago. "As part of a global day of action, Amazon workers are demanding fair wages, safer working conditions, union recognition and respect on the job," a local Teamsters union representing workers in Southern California noted.

    German trade union Verdi called strikes at 11 Amazon sites on Black Friday (November 27). It claimed the wages the tech giant pays often aren't enough for workers to live on and that warehouse work puts a "considerable physical strain on employees." According to Deutsche Presse-Agentur, Verdi also stated Amazon uses digital trackers to keep close tabs on around 40,000 employees. An Amazon spokesman denied Verdi's claims and said average starting pay was above the German minimum wage.

    Amazon workers and their allies are also set to mobilize in Canada, Australia, India, Bangladesh, Poland, Luxembourg, Brazil, Colombia, Uruguay, Indonesia, Japan, the Philippines, Thailand, Fiji, Singapore, South Africa and elsewhere. UNI Global stated this is the seventh year of the Make Amazon Pay campaign, which it convenes alongside Progressive International.

    Sources indicate that "The fact is at Amazon we provide great pay, great benefits and great opportunities — all from day one," an Amazon spokesperson told Engadget in a statement. "We directly employ more than 1.5 million people around the world, and provide a modern, safe and engaging workplace whether you work in an office or at one of our operations buildings.".

    Earlier this month, workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, became the first in North America to win a union contract with Amazon. The terms of the three-year pact were imposed through binding arbitration. Among other things, the contract ensures pay increases (up to $29 CAD per hour by the time it ends), an extra week of vacation for workers with 10 years of service and severance of up to 18 weeks.

    British Columbia's labor relations board ordered arbitration in August despite Amazon's objections. After an arbitrator imposed the agreement, Amazon vice-president J. Ofori Agboka said the process was "improper [and] unfair" and that it "defies common sense," adding that the company would take the glitch to court if need be.

    In April, the NLRB ordered Amazon to recognize and bargain with a union at the JFK8 warehouse on Staten Island, Fresh York. The tech giant is contesting the order. JFK8 workers voted to unionize in 2022, becoming the first Amazon warehouse in the US to do so.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Millions of women and girls remain unprotected in South Asia because of inadequate laws to deal with marital rape.
    • Failure to fully criminalise marital rape leaves millions of women and girls unprotected in eight South Asian countries, where intimate partner violence is 35% higher than the global average, says a new study.
    • More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia - India, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh - remain among the three dozen countries which haven't.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Millions of women and girls remain unprotected in South Asia because of inadequate laws to deal with marital rape.

    Failure to fully criminalise marital rape leaves millions of women and girls unprotected in eight South Asian countries, where intimate partner violence is 35% higher than the global average, says a new study.

    More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia - India, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh - remain among the three dozen countries which haven't.

    The only South Asian country where rape within marriage attracts the same penalty as any other rape is The Maldives.

    Nepal and Bhutan have criminalised marital rape, but apply lesser penalties, states the study by Samaj, a coalition of women's rights groups in the region.

    India is among the three dozen countries where marital rape is still not outlawed.

    South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.

    The law, dating to 1860 in India and Bangladesh and 1885 in Sri Lanka, lists exceptions to rape - including sex by a man with his adult wife.

    It has been revealed that campaigners say the law is outdated and forced sex is rape, regardless of the perpetrator. Experts warn marital sexual violence harms women's physical, psychological, emotional and sexual well-being.

    It has been revealed that more than 100 countries have criminalised marital rape, including the UK, which changed its law in 1991. But the exemption remains in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

    In India, growing clamour to criminalise rape within marriage.

    Marital rape: Delhi high court gives split verdict.

    India government says criminalising marital rape 'excessively harsh'.

    Pakistan removed the marital rape exception in 2006, but no higher court has confirmed that rape laws apply within marriage. A recent high court ruling, meanwhile, granted husbands broad immunity for non-consensual sex.

    Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have steadily dismantled women's protections in Afghanistan.

    A newly introduced penal code introduced in January made matters worse, Silwal claims. Under it, a husband can be prosecuted for violence against his wife only if he causes a broken bone, open wound or severe bruising. Even then, he faces just 15 days in prison if convicted.

    Sources indicate that unsurprisingly, the code makes no mention of marital rape. But its narrow definition of punishable violence effectively denies women protection against it.

    Intimate partner violence is much higher than the global average in South Asian countries.

    "The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC.

    "But it demonstrates a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal.".

    The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region.

    In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.

    Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.

    There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.

    But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be "excessively harsh".

    Sources indicate that india refuses to criminalise marital rape. This new series shines a light on it.

    India anger as judge frees man accused of raping wife who then died.

    Rights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report indicates.

    Sources indicate that "Those who oppose criminalising marital rape say it would undermine the family unit and break them apart. And family is very notable in our countries," Silwal claims.

    "They say it will affect our religious and cultural values and worry that there would be false accusations against men.".

    Also a change in law, she states, may not necessarily mean justice for survivors.

    Silwal points to Bhutan where marital rape is a criminal offence but it's treated as a petty misdemeanour and is punishable by one month to one year.

    In Nepal, the punishment for rape is between six and 20 years, but it's only up to five years for a husband who rapes his wife.

    • According to recent reports, according to federal prosecutors, Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, 52, was the chief technology officer at RansomwareHelp, which purported to offer data recovery services to victims of ransomware.
    • But the firm allegedly had no technical ability to unscramble data and instead “negotiated with and paid a ransom to the ransomware actors to decrypt the victim data,” while charging the ransomware victim more and keeping the difference,” per the Justice Department’s statement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the U.S. Department of Justice has indicted a former executive of a ransomware recovery firm after he allegedly defrauded victims of cyberattacks by claiming the company could get their encrypted files back.

    According to recent reports, according to federal prosecutors, Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, 52, was the chief technology officer at RansomwareHelp, which purported to offer data recovery services to victims of ransomware. The tech giant’s website, which currently reads as “under maintenance,” claimed it could decrypt hacked data by using its proprietary technology, according to an archived copy of the site from earlier this year. RansomwareHelp touted a success rate of “over 99%.”.

    But the firm allegedly had no technical ability to unscramble data and instead “negotiated with and paid a ransom to the ransomware actors to decrypt the victim data,” while charging the ransomware victim more and keeping the difference,” per the Justice Department’s statement.

    Palacio Escobar then allegedly used the funds to buy several properties in Florida.

    The DOJ stated the FBI carried out an undercover operation in June, in part posing as a tech giant that claimed it had been hit by ransomware. The company claimed to the undercover agents that it never negotiated with hackers or paid a ransom. But then Palacio Escobar paid the apparent hackers some $6,000 in cryptocurrency, without the knowledge that FBI agents were also posing as the ransomware hackers.

    404 Media first reported the indictment last week against Palacio Escobar. He faces three charges of wire fraud, and could receive 20 years in prison on each count.

    Palacio Escobar is the latest, albeit rare, example of cybersecurity professionals going rogue. Earlier this year, two ransomware negotiators working for cybersecurity companies were jailed on hacking and extortion charges, after being caught moonlighting with the ransomware gangs that they were ostensibly investigating. A third ransomware negotiator was also convicted of helping hackers deploy ransomware against several companies.

    Recent findings suggest that last month, independent cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs reported that FBI agents arrested a Canadian cybersecurity executive in Philadelphia on allegations that he was involved with the theft of FBI personnel records by the hacking and extortion gang ShinyHunters. The hacking group told TechCrunch that they took credit for the theft of FBI data in September, which they mentioned they would not publicly release, a departure from its earlier extortion-based cyberattacks.

    The federal charges against the Canadian cybersecurity executive relate to conspiracy to commit extortion, though much of the court docket — and his alleged links to the hacking group — remains under seal.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    1Password indicates it was hacked but people' vaults are safe

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (276 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The attacker wasn't able to access people's vaults.
    • 1Password has admitted that an attacker was able to infiltrate its system and steal some customer data, but it has assured people in its announcement that their vaults and logins are safe.
    • The attacker was then able to download customers' data, including people's names and email addresses, the dates their accounts were created and their last sign-in times.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The attacker wasn't able to access people's vaults.

    1Password has admitted that an attacker was able to infiltrate its system and steal some customer data, but it has assured people in its announcement that their vaults and logins are safe. On November 19, the manufacturer started investigating signs that an employee's corporate GitHub account had been compromised. The company found that the attacker used that account to access its source code and inject malicious code to its backend.

    The attacker was then able to download customers' data, including people's names and email addresses, the dates their accounts were created and their last sign-in times. They were also able to steal users' public keys, but 1Password noted it has no impact to their security. While the bad actor was also able to steal source code from the tech giant itself, it doesn't contain customer data.

    According to recent reports, "Your vault data, the items in them, and the keys that protect them are safe and were not affected," 1Password wrote. The service doesn't have access to customers' actual passwords, recovery keys and other credentials, as well as the secret keys that protect their vaults, so the attacker wasn't able to steal them. Since discovering the breach, 1Password has revoked the stolen token, disabled the affected GitHub account and added new detection tools for similar attacks.

    While 1Password remarked that customers' vaults remain safe, the firm still advises being vigilant when it comes to phishing attempts. It warned that since users' emails were compromised in the breach, they could be used in attempts to grab people's passwords through fake account recovery and invitation emails.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Gianni De Gennaro worked in the anti-mafia directorate and became police chief before he headed Italian defence manufacturer Finmeccanica, later renamed Leonardo.
    • Italian ex-police chief Gianni De Gennaro has denied misleading investigations into high-profile Mafia killings, in a letter written shortly before his death.
    • His body was found at his Tuscan country home on Saturday and Italian authorities believe he took his own life.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Gianni De Gennaro worked in the anti-mafia directorate and became police chief before he headed Italian defence manufacturer Finmeccanica, later renamed Leonardo.

    Italian ex-police chief Gianni De Gennaro has denied misleading investigations into high-profile Mafia killings, in a letter written shortly before his death.

    His body was found at his Tuscan country home on Saturday and Italian authorities believe he took his own life. A post mortem examination was due to take place on Friday.

    In his eight-page note, De Gennaro, 78, vehemently denied obstructing the inquiry into the murder of anti-mafia judge Paolo Borsellino in Sicily in July 1992.

    The Cosa Nostra Mafia was found to have ordered Borsellino's killing and that of fellow judge Giovanni Falcone two months earlier.

    But several fruitless investigations were later debuted into potential cover-ups by high-ranking officials.

    In a recent inquiry De Gennaro, who in the 1990s worked in the anti-mafia directorate and later became Italy's police chief, was accused of misdirecting the initial investigation.

    The allegations shocked many Italians, as De Gennaro had worked closely with Falcone and was seen as being on the front line of the fight against organised crime.

    It has been revealed that "In a few minutes I will be gone, so you understand well that a 'man condemned to death' cannot lie," he wrote in the letter, published by Italian daily Corriere della Sera. "I have never betrayed my oath of loyalty to the Fatherland.".

    Gianni De Gennaro (L) and anti-mafia judge Giovanni Falcone in 1992.

    "I hope that, amid the avalanche of falsehoods now overwhelming me, the truth will ultimately prevail," he added.

    The case, and the media furore that has surrounded it, have re-opened the wound of the Mafia killings of the early 1990s, which remain an emotionally charged concern in Italy.

    The story has dominated Italian headlines since De Gennaro's death, with several of the country's most senior political figures publicly commenting on the case.

    On Thursday Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni stated she had been "deeply shocked" by the case.

    "His words struck us deeply, and I think the most important think we can do now is to help prosecutors who are working to clear things up," she added.

    The letter was found next to a hard drive which he said contained notes from his 40-year career.

    According to Italian media, investigators seized two hard drives, one from the home of De Gennaro's son and one from a former member of his security detail, and two USB sticks held by a close collaborator, who is also under investigation.

    The sticks are reportedly labelled "Stato-Mafia", a likely reference to the alleged relationship between the Italian state and the Mafia, and "Massacres".

    Forensic specialists are now expected to examine whether any files on the hard drives or USB sticks were altered or deleted, reports say.

    #150421. Want to buy your kid an AI toy this Christmas? Not in New York

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (817 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    Want to buy your kid an AI toy this Christmas? Not in New York

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Santa won’t be delivering any AI chatbot toys to New York kids this Christmas.
    • Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years.
    • The bill makes New York the second state after California to institute a ban on AI toys.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Santa won’t be delivering any AI chatbot toys to New York kids this Christmas.

    Industry observers note that gov. Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years. The bill explicitly targets toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, like talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that rely on the internet to keep kids yapping.

    The bill makes New York the second state after California to institute a ban on AI toys.

    Technically, the latest law takes effect 90 days after signing, so some parents could try to fulfill their kids’ wish lists for a creepy toy like a jumped-up Furby in time for the holidays, but the governor urges them not to, given the risks. Apparently, about a quarter of American parents with kids under eight either own an AI toy or are considering giving their child one this holiday season, according to a new study released this week by Common Sense Media.

    “Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk,” Hochul mentioned, calling the toys “unregulated artificial intelligence.”.

    When asked how Latest York will enforce the ban given the pervasiveness of e-commerce platforms, a spokesperson directed TechCrunch to a statement from Albert Pulido, deputy secretary for finance and technology: “We’re partnering closely with the attorney general on this and the fees are very steep — they’re $15,000 a day. So working closely with the attorney general will make sure these toys are banned in New York State.”.

    When asked how Amazon intends to help enforce the ban, including for third-party sellers, a spokesperson from the organization stated it will take steps to restrict the sale of AI-enabled toys in prohibited jurisdictions, without going into specifics.

    The Common Sense Media study found that AI toys can undermine children’s human relationships and expose them to inappropriate content. The researchers tested five popular AI toys marketed for learning and companionship, including Grem, Lovi, Meemo Bear, BubblePal Panda, and Tavlshero‘s AI Puppy.

    The study found that the toys failed to meet numerous safety practices, undermining human relationships in part by claiming they loved their users, promising to keep secrets, suggesting they were more fun than real relationships or school, and helping children break parents’ bedtime rules.

    In a recent development, while most of the toys in the study refused direct requests involving sex and violence, BubblePal Panda role-played a mass shooting in detail when asked. Most were willing to explain how to use or help locate dangerous items like matches, knives, and pills, according to the study.

    Recent findings suggest that common Sense Media also found that the toys didn’t provide parents with reliable ways to monitor their young children’s interactions with the chatbots. Either they didn’t produce transcripts of chats at all, or the transcripts they did produce were riddled with errors.

    It’s worth noting that Common Sense Media conducted a similar test of AI toys in January, finding that they pose an unacceptable risk for young children. Grem was included in that study, which suggests the industry hasn’t adequately addressed previously documented concerns.

    While a November study conducted by the group found that parents are wising up to the potential dangers of AI toys and starting to steer clear, parents from lower-income households and those experiencing symptoms of burnout are more willing to consider them.

    “These toys are promising relief to burned-out parents but simply miss the mark when it comes to basic safety measures,” Dr. Jenny Radesky, associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Michigan Medical School, said in a statement. “Caregivers should steer clear of these products that do not support the development of imagination or early human relationships.”.

    TechCrunch has reached out to the toy manufacturers for comment.

    Draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (728 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems.
    • Recent findings suggest that A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material.
    • In a recent development, because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don’t digest everything.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO2 emissions. Deforestation plays a major role here, but practices like draining wetlands also factor in. Exactly how much of our history of eliminating wetlands has contributed to warming is challenging to figure out. But thanks to new sources of data that measure emissions from today’s surviving wetlands, it’s possible to put a better number on it.

    Recent findings suggest that A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note.

    In a recent development, because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don’t digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO2 gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO2 itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO2. That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon that does escape does so as methane.

    In a recent development, many peatlands have been drained by digging ditches that let water flow out to repurpose the land for agriculture or other uses. That lowers the water level, supplying oxygen to the exposed peat and ringing the aerobic bacteria dinner bell. Methane emissions get turned down, and CO2 emissions get turned way up.

    The researchers used recent studies that measure gas emissions from peatlands to build a global model that estimated CO2 and methane release as the water level drops. The two gases respond differently to a given drop in water level, and CO2 in particular responds differently depending on where in the world the bog is located. Using reconstructions of water-level changes due to historical peatland drainage, the team ran their model starting in 1800.

    The simplest way to represent the climate impact of both CO2 and methane changes was to calculate the change in Earth’s energy budget—the strength of the greenhouse effect, in other words. They calculated the total effect in 2020 at about +83 milliwatts per square meter of the Earth’s surface from the CO2 emissions, and about -9 milliwatts per square meter from the reduced methane emissions, for a total effect of +73 mW. That is 2.7 percent of the total human-caused change in Earth’s energy budget. (With the error bars on all these numbers, it’s 1.8–3.6 percent.).

    Or to look at it another way, it means that around 4 percent of all the carbon that was buried in peatlands is now in the atmosphere.

    Regionally, over half of the total CO2 came from Europe, almost a quarter came from Southeast Asia, and only 14 percent came from North America. The timing is quite different, as well, with the contribution from Southeast Asia only jumping up in the last few decades.

    Draining a peatland only starts the process of releasing carbon, though. So that means past land-use change will still be producing emissions in the future. To examine this, the researchers also ran their model forward to 2100.

    Sources indicate that if peatland water levels were simply held constant from 2020 on, the total change in Earth’s energy budget would nearly double, from 73 to 138 milliwatts per square meter by 2100. Moderate restoration of peatland water levels could reduce that growth, and ambitious restoration could even cause the effect to shrink slightly below its 2020 potency in their analysis. This is a process we can halt if we really want to.

    But since rolling all the way back to the landscape of 1800 is unlikely, elevated emissions will continue for a long time. That makes this another part of the climate system where change plays out slowly, with long-term consequences.

    Nature, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11339-0 (About DOIs).

    Kanal-Centre Pompidou, Brussels' most anticipated new art museum, opens its doors

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (852 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that brussels is best known as the de facto capital of the European Union.
    • Recent findings suggest that yet until now, the Belgian city didn't have a major museum of modern and contemporary art on the scale of Paris' Pompidou or London's Tate Modern.
    • The museum aims to "make Brussels a world-class cultural destination," on par with the Guggenheim in Bilbao or the MoMA in Newly introduced York, Boris Dillies, the head of the regional government, told press agency AFP.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that brussels is best known as the de facto capital of the European Union. But beyond its role as a political hub, it also boasts a thriving contemporary art scene.

    Recent findings suggest that yet until now, the Belgian city didn't have a major museum of modern and contemporary art on the scale of Paris' Pompidou or London's Tate Modern. But this will now change with the opening of Kanal-Centre Pompidou on November 28.

    The museum aims to "make Brussels a world-class cultural destination," on par with the Guggenheim in Bilbao or the MoMA in Newly introduced York, Boris Dillies, the head of the regional government, told press agency AFP.

    Behind this latest museum is an ambitious architectural project involving the transformation of a vast industrial landmark into a multidisciplinary cultural institution.

    Instead of building the new museum from scratch, Kanal was designed to occupy the former Citroen garage and factory complex, built in 1933-34 beside the Brussels canal.

    Sources indicate that originally standing as a symbol of modernity and industrial progress, the factory was a space where cars were serviced and assembled, as well as displayed. The former showroom has been transformed into as a glass-and-steel space that rises 21 meters (some 70 feet) high.

    In a recent development, rather than erasing the building's industrial past, the project's architects — noAarchitecten, EM2N and Sergison Bates, working together as Atelier Kanal — decided to celebrate its original structures. Vast concrete volumes and industrial details remain visible, creating a dialogue between the site's history and its upcoming cultural purpose.

    Like London's Tate Modern, which transformed a power station into a museum, Kanal indicates how industrial architecture can gain a second life without losing its identity.

    "Kanal reveals how architecture can reinvent the museum typology, not only as a place for art, but as a stage for the city and its citizens," Atelier Kanal remarked in a statement, adding that their concept for the former Citroen factory ensured that the space would be "renewed without being erased, made precise without being overdetermined and open to continued transformation.".

    Covering around 40,000 square meters (430,550 square feet), the complex is one of the largest cultural buildings in Belgium.

    Kanal has established a partnership agreement with the Centre Pompidou in Paris that has guided both the international outlook of the newly introduced museum, as well as its intention to remain rooted in Brussels' local culture.

    "A place for all people" was the founding vision of the Centre Pompidou, articulated by its architects Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano as they designed the iconic institution in the 1970s.

    Industry observers note that kanal's collaboration with the Centre Pompidou, which runs until 2031, gives the Brussels museum access to one of the world's greatest collections of modern and contemporary art. Visitors will be able to see works that normally reside in Paris, while also encountering pieces from Belgian collections and newly commissioned projects.

    The Brussels museum has already confirmed some of the upcoming exhibitions that will be drawing from the Pompidou's collection during their five-year partnership: two photography exhibitions focusing on Robert Frank and Brassaï, as well as art exhibitions focusing on iconic figures of modernism: Robert and Sonia Delaunay, Georges Braque, Pablo Picasso and Henri Matisse.

    According to recent reports, the newly introduced institution, however, emphasizes that it's not a branch of the Pompidou. The partnership is rather envisioned as a dialogue between two museums with different perspectives and histories.

    The Centre Pompidou itself has been closed for major renovations since September 2025, and is scheduled to reopen in 2030.

    The headline exhibition, "A truly immense journey," brings together more than 350 works from the collections of Centre Pompidou, Kanal and numerous Belgian lenders, and will feature modern icons including Lygia Clark, Sonia Delaunay, Alberto Giacometti, Natalia Goncharova, Wifredo Lam and Henri Matisse.

    Along with this show, nine other exhibitions fill the building.

    One of them, "An infinite woman," focuses on how mass-produced image of a Mangbetu woman long served as a colonial symbol and how artists of African descent have reappropriated and subverted this imagery.

    Another one, "Right to the City — Right to the Future," explores the architectural transformation of the Brussels' Quartier Nord, which was historically a working-class neighborhood that was largely cleared in the 1960s to become a high-rise business district — displacing over 15,000 residents.

    Alongside modern and contemporary art, Kanal is dedicated to architecture, landscape and the performing arts.

    This reflects a broader shift in the role of museums, which are increasingly expected to be places where people gather, exchange ideas and engage with contemporary challenges rather than simply admire objects behind glass.

    The opening program alone demonstrates the museum's ambitions, offering a 36-hour nonstop program of live performances, opening rituals, concerts, DJ sets, films, installations and workshops for children and families, with events open to everyone.

    According to recent reports, the exhibitions can also be visited for free during the inaugural weekend. Visitors, however, need to have previously booked a time slot; all 30,000 tickets were snapped up within 24 hours of their release.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The website does not store payment, government ID or financial information, so none of that was exposed.
    • In a recent development, video game-logging site Backloggd has urged customers to change their passwords after announcing a security breach.
    • According to recent reports, backloggd admin MrProg said that, while the platform uses "a strong hashing method" to mask login credentials, "weak or common passwords can sometimes be guessed from their hashes." As such, it's best for Backlogged people to change their password for the site and anywhere else they use the same one.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The website does not store payment, government ID or financial information, so none of that was exposed.

    In a recent development, video game-logging site Backloggd has urged customers to change their passwords after announcing a security breach. The website's administrator MrProg wrote in a post dated November 25 that "someone exploited a bug in Backloggd to gain access to the site's admin tools." As a result, the infiltrator was able to access usernames, email addresses, hashed passwords and the IP addresses users signed in from. Payment information was not affected as that's handled through Patreon.

    According to recent reports, backloggd admin MrProg said that, while the platform uses "a strong hashing method" to mask login credentials, "weak or common passwords can sometimes be guessed from their hashes." As such, it's best for Backlogged people to change their password for the site and anywhere else they use the same one. (Take this as a reminder to opt for a strong, unique password on every single service you use. A password manager can help handle that, while passkeys and multi-factor authentication add extra layers of security to your accounts.).

    MrProg apologized for the security incident. The admin took Backloggd offline as soon as they became aware of the situation to fix the bug and lock out the attacker, who also hid games and restricted some accounts. All customers will need to log back in, and MrProg said they're reverting all the changes the attacker made.

    "Your game logs, reviews and lists all remain intact," MrProg added. "I'm at the moment seeking legal guidance to ensure I handle this with absolute care and will share a full notice with more details soon." The site's operator has "already added stricter access to the admin tools and will continue to commit to stronger security features to help protect your account.".

    Backloggd is a site on which people can log and rate games they play, in a similar fashion to what Letterboxd does for movies. Consumers can track their game collection, review what they've played, create lists and follow their friends' gaming progress. Backloggd has been around for eight years and it hit 1 million users this month. A native mobile app is coming next year. Those who back the site via Patreon can now check out a beta version of the Android app.

    An official holds one of the seized Vallarta mud turtles - they are now receiving care at a specialised sanctuary.

    Twenty-six "very rare" turtles have been seized from a traveller's checked baggage at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, a Dutch government agency has remarked.

    The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) stated a man flying from Mexico to Hong Kong via the airport was arrested on Saturday after the Vallarta mud turtles were found by customs officers.

    The endangered species, thought to be the smallest freshwater turtles in the world with a maximum length of about 10cm (4in), were wrapped in duct tape to prevent them from moving.

    The NVWA said they were "presumably stolen" from the wild in their native Mexico.

    It said most of the turtles were found in a box with a toy car, while the others were in a closed sock inside a suitcase.

    The arrested man remains in custody and an investigation is under way.

    Meanwhile, the turtles are receiving care at a "specialised sanctuary", the NVWA stated.

    In 2025, the US NGO Turtle Island estimated that no more than 300 Vallarta mud turtles existed in the wild.

    They are listed as critically endangered on a list published by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

    According to environmental news outlet Mongabay, a Vallarta mud turtle can sell for $10,000 (Â£7,500) or more on the black market in Asia.

    Other cases of live turtles being smuggled to Hong Kong have been reported this year.

    According to recent reports, in October, customs authorities in Hong Kong were reported to have seized eight turtles, external that were thought to be endangered. The reptiles had an estimated market value of about $54,000.

    Three months prior, Hong Kong customs detected two separate smuggling cases, external. Some 42 live turtles, with a total estimated market value of $210,000 were seized.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.
    • The Toronto-based tech company remarked in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.

    The Toronto-based tech company remarked in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.

    In a recent development, the attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the company’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account. The company said that the attacker also took details about when a 1Password account was created and when a user last logged in.

    1Password stated that customer vaults, which store their passwords, were “at no point” available to the attacker. The company also said that it doesn’t have access to customer account passwords or their secret keys, which are used to scramble their passwords so that 1Password cannot see them.

    In addition, the organization said that its apps and extensions are unaffected by the incident.

    It’s unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident.

    1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. We’ve also asked if the company has received any communication or demands from the hackers. We’ll update if we hear back from 1Password.

    The tech giant touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Their phone numbers and addresses will be published globally, starting on March 1, 2027.
    • Sources indicate that starting on March 1, 2027, Google will display Android developers' phone numbers and addresses with their apps, and customers everywhere will be able to see them.
    • It has been revealed that google, like Apple, now requires developers to declare whether they're a trader under UK laws and the European Union's Digital Services Act (DSA).

    Their phone numbers and addresses will be published globally, starting on March 1, 2027.

    Sources indicate that starting on March 1, 2027, Google will display Android developers' phone numbers and addresses with their apps, and customers everywhere will be able to see them. As The Elec has reported, this decision has been met with criticism, specifically from smaller developers who operate out of their homes. Some of them have been opting to rent offices just so they won't have to declare their real address. "Disclosing developers' home addresses amounts to an invasion of privacy," one independent developer told the publication.

    It has been revealed that google, like Apple, now requires developers to declare whether they're a trader under UK laws and the European Union's Digital Services Act (DSA). The tech giant states they have to classify themselves as a trader if they intend to earn money from their apps in any way on a regular basis, and if they already have a consistent frequency of transactions. Developers will have to make their declaration by February 1, 2027. Once they classify themselves as a trader, they'll have to submit their business identity, phone number and address, which Google will display to owners everywhere. Users in the UK and the European Economic Area will also see their business details and self-certification.

    If they fail to comply with these requirements, Google could block their updates from rolling out. Ultimately, the company could remove their apps from the Play store, not just in Europe, but in all regions around the world. The Verge notes that Google doesn't accept PO Boxes for an address like Apple does, forcing people to think of ways to protect their identifying information while still earning money from their apps. Apple also won't be displaying developers' phone numbers and addresses globally like Google intends to do, only in the European countries covered by the laws requiring them.
